$purpose: The safety number is the value two people read aloud to each other to confirm that no key was
substituted between them. Its only job is to differ when the identity keys differ, so any two
implementations that disagree turn a verification into theatre: the numbers on the two screens
do not match, both users conclude they are under attack, and nothing is wrong. The reverse is
worse and is what these vectors exist to prevent — two inputs that should differ producing one
number, which is a verification that confirms nothing while looking exactly like one that did.
iOS carried a second implementation of this until 2026-08-27 (582-line neighbourhood in
SafetyNumberView, under a comment promising it matched the core). It now calls the core, and
these vectors are what a third client is checked against instead of a comment.
$construction: 1. Both ids must be non-empty and decodable as hex. Otherwise there is NO number — see $refusal.
2. Sort the two ids as STRINGS (not as bytes, and with no case normalisation), so both sides
agree on the order. A client that lowercases before sorting will disagree with one that
does not, on any pair whose ids differ in case.
5. Take the first 24 bytes as 12 big-endian u16 pairs; each is rendered as 5 decimal digits, zero-padded, and joined with single spaces: 71 characters.

The range that occurs is 00000-65535, not 00000-99999: a group is a u16. The core applies a `% 100000` that can never fire; it is a width guard for a future wider chunk, not a reduction. A client that omits it produces identical output today. The number carries 192 bits, and the five-digit groups overstate that — say 192 when reasoning about collisions.
5. Take the first 24 bytes as 12 big-endian u16 pairs; each becomes (pair % 100000) rendered
as 5 decimal digits, zero-padded. Join the 12 groups with single spaces: 71 characters.
The 1024 rounds are deliberate cost against brute-forcing a key whose device id collides in
the displayed digits; a client that runs a different number of rounds produces a different
number for every input, which is the loudest possible failure and therefore the safe one.
$refusal: An id the implementation cannot read must yield no number at all — not an empty string that a
UI might render, and above all not a number computed from substituted bytes.
Until 2026-08-27 the core decoded with `unwrap_or_default()`, so an unreadable id silently
became an empty one, and an empty id is valid input that produces a real-looking 60-digit
value. Every broken id therefore collapsed onto the SAME number: 'abc', 'zzzz' and '' all
matched each other against a given peer. Two people whose ids failed to decode would have
been shown matching numbers and would have concluded the session was verified.
Empty is refused by name rather than allowed to decode cleanly, because it is the value the
old collapse produced and the one two broken clients would most easily both supply.

vectors.note: adjacent ids: one bit apart in the input, unrelated in the output
the pair the core's own unit tests use, so a change there and a change here cannot pass separately
a is the string-greater id, so the sort swaps the concatenation order
real device ids from the three-simulator stand; the leading group 25250 has a zero that a naive formatter drops

symmetry: compute(a, b) == compute(b, a) for every vector above. A client that produces different
numbers depending on which side asks has not implemented the sort, and its users will see
mismatched numbers on every single verification.

refused.note: empty decodes cleanly — refused by name
either side, not just the first
